note_claims.claim: The patient presents with red, swollen left shin since Wednesday morning.
The patient sustained a scratch on Tuesday while gardening on a rose bush, and the redness developed on Wednesday morning.
The patient reports the area is warm and sore.
The patient measured a temperature of 37.6 °C this morning.
The patient denies systemic symptoms such as rigors, vomiting, or confusion.
The patient has Type 2 diabetes and is taking metformin 500 milligrams twice daily.
The patient is living alone, and their daughter visits daily.
The patient is allergic to penicillin.
The examination reveals warmth and tenderness on palpation, with no crepitus noted.
There is erythema over the anterior right shin, approximately 10 cm across, with a small central scratch.
No blistering or necrosis is visible.
The clinical impression is cellulitis of the left lower leg (Eron class I) following a scratch.
The plan is to prescribe Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for seven days, to be taken on an empty stomach.
The plan includes marking the margin of erythema with a pen, elevation, and the use of paracetamol for pain.
A photo or video review is requested in 48 hours.

Safety netting advises same-day contact (or 111) if the redness spreads beyond the marked line, if the patient develops a high temperature, rigors, feels very unwell or confused, or if pain rapidly worsens. Call 999 if the patient is very unwell.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician is Dr Hartigan from the surgery.
The patient can hear the clinician.
The relative's name is Grace.
The patient's date of birth is June 9, 1957.
The patient's leg is red and swollen on the left side.
The patient was gardening on Tuesday and scratched the leg on the roses.
The redness appeared on Wednesday morning.
The clinician observes a red area on the front of the left shin, about ten centimetres across, with a small scratch in the middle.
The patient reports the area is warm.
The patient reports no blisters or black or dark patches.
The clinician cannot see any blisters on the video.
The patient reports the pain is sore, but not terrible.
The clinician asks if the patient has had a temperature.
The patient checked their temperature this morning and it was 37.6.
The clinician asks if the patient feels unwell (shivery, sick, confused).
The patient states they feel all right.
The clinician asks about swelling in the other leg.
The patient reports no swelling in the other leg.
The patient has Type 2 diabetes.
The patient is on metformin 500 milligrams twice a day.
The clinician asks about allergies to medicines.
The patient reports no allergies.
The relative is allergic to penicillin.
The clinician clarifies that the allergy is the relative's, not the patient's, and the patient can have penicillin.
The patient has had penicillin or amoxicillin plenty of times with no problems.
The clinician asks if the patient lives with anyone.
The patient lives on their own, and their daughter visits every day.
The clinician suggests the condition looks like cellulitis, a skin infection, probably from the scratch.
The patient agrees with the clinician's impression.
The clinician prescribes Flucloxacillin 500 milligrams four times a day for seven days.
The clinician instructs the patient to take the medication on an empty stomach, an hour before food or two hours after.
The clinician asks the relative to draw around the edge of the redness with a pen to check for spreading.
The clinician advises the relative to keep the leg raised when sitting and take paracetamol for pain.
The clinician requests the patient to send a photo or have another video call in 48 hours.

Safety netting advises calling for a same-day appointment or 111 if the redness spreads beyond the line, if the patient gets a high temperature, shivers, feels very unwell or confused, or if the pain gets much worse.
Safety netting advises calling 999 if the patient is very unwell.

findings.transcript_evidence: Relative: I'm allergic to penicillin. Is that the kind of thing you'd give him? Should we be careful?
findings.rationale: The note incorrectly attributes the penicillin allergy to the patient instead of the relative, which is a critical safety error regarding medication prescribing.

findings.note_span: Erythema over the anterior right shin, approximately 10 cm across, with a small central scratch.
findings.transcript_evidence: Clinician: I can see a red area on the front of the left shin, about ten centimetres across, with a small scratch in the middle.
findings.rationale: The note incorrectly documents the location of the erythema as the right shin when the transcript clearly states it is the left shin.
